opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important things we can do, honestly. There's a real temptation in robotics to show the highlight reel: the perfect pick, the flawless walk across the warehouse floor, the demo that went right on the fifteenth take. That's understandable, because you're raising money and you want people excited. But it creates a distorted picture of where the technology actually is, and that hurts everybody in the long run.

When you're open about failures, a few good things happen. First, you set realistic expectations with customers. If someone deploys a robot believing it'll work a hundred percent of the time, and it works ninety-two percent of the time, they're disappointed and they lose trust. If you tell them up front, "Here's where it struggles, here are the edge cases, here's how we handle recovery," then ninety-two percent can be a great outcome, because they've planned for it.

Second, failures are where the learning is. In robotics the long tail is everything. The weird lighting, the crumpled package, the object that's slightly reflective, the person who walks in at an unexpected angle. If you treat those as embarrassments to hide, you don't build the culture or the tooling to capture them, analyze them, and feed them back into the system. The teams that make real progress treat every failure as data.

And third, I think it matters for the field as a whole. When companies overpromise, you get these hype cycles where investors and the public get burned, and then funding dries up for everyone, including the people doing careful, serious work. Being candid about what doesn't work yet is how you build durable credibility and keep the industry on a steady path instead of boom and bust.

So my view is that honesty isn't just an ethical nicety. It's a practical engineering and business advantage. The robots get better faster when you're willing to look hard at where they fall short.

r001.rationale: The candidate says failures should be captured, analyzed, and fed back into the system, and that examining where robots fall short helps them improve—clearly communicating that honesty enables teams to address technical problems.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually one of the most important things we can do, and honestly it's something the field has been bad at for a long time. If you only ever see the highlight reel, the demo video where the robot nails the task on the twentieth take, you get a completely distorted picture of where the technology really is. And that distortion hurts everyone. It hurts investors who set expectations that can't be met, it hurts customers who deploy something expecting it to work ninety-nine percent of the time when it's really at seventy, and it hurts the engineers who end up under pressure to hide problems instead of fix them.

When you're honest about failures, a couple of good things happen. First, you actually learn faster. The failure cases are where all the information is. If a robot drops an object or freezes in front of a door it's never seen before, that's the data point that tells you what to work on next. If you bury that, you're throwing away the most valuable signal you have.

Second, it builds trust, and robotics needs trust more than almost any other technology because these are physical systems operating around people. If a company says "here's what our system can't do yet, here's where it struggles," I believe them when they tell me what it can do. The companies that oversell eventually get caught, and then nobody believes anything they say.

And third, I think it makes the whole field more collaborative. When people share what went wrong, other teams don't have to rediscover the same dead ends. Some of the most useful conversations I've had have been with people saying "we tried that, here's why it didn't work." That's worth more than ten polished demos.

So yes, it's uncomfortable, especially when you're fundraising or trying to close a deal. But I think the long-term health of the technology depends on it. The hype cycle in robotics has burned people before, and the way you avoid repeating that is by being straight about where things actually stand.

r001.rationale: The response says failure cases reveal what to work on next and that hiding them prevents engineers from fixing problems, clearly linking honesty to addressing technical issues.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s essential. If we’re not honest about where robots fail, we’re not going to solve the right problems. A demo can look fantastic, but the real question is what happens when that robot has to work all day in an environment you don’t control. Where does it get stuck? When does a person have to step in?

Those failures are valuable feedback. Being open about them helps engineers improve the technology, and it helps customers set realistic expectations. You can build trust by saying, “Here’s what it does well today, here’s where it struggles, and here’s what we’re working on.” Pretending it already works perfectly just makes the gap between expectations and reality harder to close.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that without honesty about where robots fail, the team will not solve the right problems, and that failures provide feedback for improving the technology.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s essential. If you’re not honest about where a robot fails, you can’t really make it better. You can put together a great demo, but the real question is, what happens when that robot has to work every day in an environment you don’t control?

And customers need to understand those limits, too. If you tell them exactly what the robot can do, where it struggles, and when a person needs to step in, you can build trust and learn together. If you oversell it, even a useful robot can look like a disappointment. Being honest about failures gives you a much better foundation for progress.

r001.rationale: The response says that without honesty about where a robot fails, you cannot make it better, communicating that honesty helps address its real technical problems.
